notes.meaning: Job speaks about the shared weakness of every human being. Anyone born into this world lives only a short time and faces plenty of sorrow. Job brings up this common misery to ask God for pity on his own painful life.

Human life blossoms like a flower, but it soon fades and withers away. It is also like a quick shadow that races across the ground and disappears into the dark. Because life is so fragile and brief, people cannot put their lasting trust in earthly things.

Job wonders why the almighty God would fix His gaze on such a frail creature. It seems surprising that the Lord would call a weak, dying mortal into court to judge him. Job uses this thought to ask God to treat him with mercy instead of strict justice.

No human being can produce something completely pure out of a nature that is sinful from birth. People inherit moral weakness and fault from their ancestors, making every person imperfect. Because of this, only God's mercy and cleansing power can make a person truly right before Him.

differ.view: Some Anglicans read this verse as describing bodily weakness and ceremonial uncleanness rather than the doctrine of inherited guilt.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Douay-Rheims translation reads the second question as pointing to God alone as the only One who can make the unclean clean.

notes.meaning: God has already set the exact span of each person's life on earth. He knows the count of our months and has placed a limit that no one can cross. Human life cannot be stretched out beyond the boundary that the Lord has decided.

Job pleads with God to look away from him and ease up on His heavy discipline. Like a hired worker who looks forward to resting when the day's hard labor is done, man longs for a little peace before life ends. Job asks for a brief breathing spell before he reaches the end of his days.

A cut-down tree still has hope because its roots can send up fresh green shoots. Even if its trunk seems dead and rotted in the dirt, the mere scent of moisture will cause it to bud like a young sapling. Job uses the stubborn renewal of plant life to contrast how differently death treats human beings.

When a human being dies, his earthly strength is completely gone, and he wastes away in the grave. Once he breathes his last breath, he vanishes from his place on earth. Unlike a fallen tree that sprouts again, a man does not return to live his physical life over again.

Just as inland waters can evaporate or a flooded riverbed can completely dry up, a person's physical life drains away. The empty river channel shows how thoroughly life disappears from the body. Once those vital streams are gone, they do not refill the earthly frame.

A person who dies lies down in the grave and does not get up again to resume earthly life. He will not wake up from this sleep as long as the present heavens and world remain. Job looks at physical death as a complete end to life in this current age.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see this verse as a flat denial of any resurrection, arguing that Job believed the dead sleep permanently in Sheol.

notes.meaning: Job longs for Sheol, the place of the dead, to serve as a secret shelter from his intense suffering. He wishes God would hide him there until the season of divine anger passes by. He asks the Lord to set an appointed time on His calendar and then remember him with favor.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Douay-Rheims Bible renders Sheol as hell, expressing Job's plea to be protected in the realm of the dead until God's wrath ends.

notes.meaning: Job asks whether a person will live again after dying, reflecting on the hope of a coming restoration. He resolves to wait patiently through all the hard days of his earthly struggle until his great renewal arrives. He finds comfort in the hope that his present trial is not the final word.

differ.view: Some evangelicals teach that Job lacked clear revelation about eternity, so his words here express mistaken human feelings rather than doctrinal truth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars understand Job's question as expecting a negative answer, expressing despair over death rather than a hope for bodily resurrection.

notes.meaning: Job envisions a day when God will summon him, and he will gladly answer the call. He trusts that the Lord will deeply yearn for the person He formed with His own hands. Even in his darkness, Job clings to the thought that the Creator will not abandon His work forever.

In his present pain, Job feels as though God is carefully tracking every step and counting each error. He pictures his sins collected and sealed up tightly in a pouch so that none of them will be forgotten or left unpunished. Yet Job brings this heavy burden to God, longing for the day when his sins will be covered and forgiven.

The strongest parts of the natural world eventually crumble, as mountains fall and rocks slide away. Constant dripping and rushing water wear down solid stones and wash away the soil. In the same way, relentless troubles and death wash away all the earthly plans and hopes that a person builds.

God completely overpowers mortal man, and the person passes away from the earth forever. In the process of death, his face changes and loses its vitality, and God sends him away to his long home. No human being has the strength to resist the Lord's final call.

Once a person dies and enters the grave, he is cut off from the events of this world. He does not know whether his children receive great honor or whether they fall into poverty and disgrace. The ties that kept him anxious about his family's earthly status have been severed.

In this dark picture of dying, the person is consumed only by the suffering of his own body and the grief of his own spirit. The dying man cannot focus on others because his own pain and sorrow overwhelm him. Job ends his speech by laying bare the raw, bitter reality of human misery and death.
